Read more US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday for high-stakes negotiations with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky , capping a high-wire weekend of shuttle diplomacy aimed at breaking a long-standing stalemate in the war. The diplomatic mission follows a three-hour meeting with Russian president Vladimir Putin in Moscow a day earlier, and represents Washington’s most direct effort to revive peace talks since the outbreak of the US-Iran war in February. The trip marks the American envoys’ first official visit to the Ukrainian capital after traveling by train from Poland, having previously made eight visits to Moscow. While details of the discussions have not yet been made public, Witkoff said the US team had been “very encouraged” by what he described as “substantive, important” dialogue in a statement made to reporters after the first round of discussions. open image in gallery Zelensky meeting with US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Kyiv on Sunday ( AFP/Getty ) White House officials added that the envoys discussed “plans for next steps”, with a formal announcement anticipated in the coming weeks. The delegation’s arrival has brought with it a temporary three-day agreement between Moscow and Kyiv to pause air strikes targeting each other’s capitals through to the end of Tuesday. The localised truce allowed the American emissaries to travel safely into Kyiv where Zelensky greeted Witkoff and Kushner in Sophia Square – just hundreds of metres from where Ukraine’s SBU intelligence headquarters were struck by a Russian drone on Friday – before hosting them at Saint Sophia Cathedral for bilateral talks. In spite of the brief lull over Kyiv and Moscow, however, intense combat continued unabated along the 1,200km front line, with Ukrainian authorities reporting at least eight civilians were killed and nearly 70 injured over the previous 24 hours. open image in gallery Aftermath of a Russian drone attack in Ukraine earlier this week ( Reuters ) Russian air defences claimed to have intercepted 258 Ukrainian drones across 14 regions in the same period. Ukrainian forces launched deep drone strikes overnight against the Ryazan oil refinery roughly 300 miles inside Russia, sparking a major fire at the facility. Russian retaliation has since pounded regional Ukrainian targets outside the capital and claimed missile strikes against two commercial cargo vessels near Odesa on Sunday, alleging they were transporting Western military supplies through the Black Sea . The ongoing violence underscores the severe friction surrounding the negotiation efforts. During Saturday’s discussions at the Kremlin, foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov stated that Putin presented a comprehensive assessment of the battlefield, expressed complete confidence in Russian advances, and insisted that any lasting peace must address the “root causes” of the conflict. open image in gallery Talks between the Kremlin and US special envoys on Saturday were described as ‘substantive, important’ conversations ( Reuters ) Mr Ushakov characterised the talks as constructive and candid, noting that discussions also touched on potential long-term economic cooperation between Washington and Moscow, although no concrete breakthroughs were announced. Previous talks were stalled over Russian refusal to compromise on its demand for Ukraine’s total withdrawal from fortified towns in the Donbas and Kyiv’s formal renunciation of Nato membership. The Kremlin’s uncompromising tone appears largely unchanged, further underscored by foreign minister Sergei Lavrov’s warning that German accusations over a foiled airport drone plot mark what is “by and large the start of a real war”. Accusing Berlin of escalating direct confrontation, the aggressive rhetoric highlights a widening rift between Moscow and European capitals even as US mediators seek common ground. In Kyiv, Ukrainian officials have expressed firm limits on what concessions they would consider. open image in gallery Kyiv officials have made it clear that Moscow is in ‘no position’ to dictate peace terms ( AFP/Getty ) Citing the extent of Russian losses, foreign minister Andrii Sybiha has argued that Moscow is in “no position” to dictate peace terms. The talks come just weeks ahead of forecasted temperature drops, with Ukrainian authorities racing to fortify municipal heating systems and shore up power generation before autumn cold sets in. A significant portion of Sunday’s talks in Kyiv are believed to have centred on Ukraine’s urgent winter energy needs following previous Russian strikes that destroyed 9GW of power generation, with national security advisers from the UK , France , and Germany expected to join expanded discussions focused on coordinating long-term energy and security guarantees. Photograph: Jay Kogler/AAP Helen Haines Helen Haines has lost both legs after alleged attack but ‘her heart and mind are in good shape’, husband says Haines is in stable condition. Surgeons tried to save her right leg but both have now been amputated due to injuries Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Tom McIlroy Political editor Wed 21 Oct 2026 02.15 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 05.41 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The independent MP Helen Haines has lost both legs but remains in a stable condition, two days after an alleged targeted attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria. Haines, the federal MP for Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg on Tuesday, but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries. Her husband, Phil Haines, provided an update on his wife’s condition at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital late on Wednesday afternoon. Composed and clear, he said his wife had survived a “horrendous incident” and faced a long road to recovery. Helen Haines loses her legs after an alleged attack. Here’s what we know so far Read more “The good news in all this is Helen is alive and she’s stable,” he said. “That is the most important thing for our family. And I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind. “Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her – her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.” Phil Haines described his wife, 65, as a fighter. The pair have been married for nearly 40 years and have three children and two grandchildren. He became emotional for a moment at the end of the statement, reflecting on his wife’s strength. Helen Haines has lost both legs but ‘heart and mind are in good shape’, husband says – video “She is a determined person who will do her best with our support and love to recover, and that is what we hope for,” he said. “We are grateful at this stage that both her heart and her mind are in good shape.” Haines asked for donations to Save the Children as his wife recovers. A special appeal has been launched by the charity. Police allege Monday’s attack was targeted, and have charged Brendan Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Nugent faced Wangaratta magistrates court earlier on Wednesday. View image in fullscreen Phil Haines and governor general Sam Mostyn speak to reporters on Wednesday afternoon. Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty Images Phil Haines was joined by the governor general, Sam Mostyn. Mostyn said she had relayed news of the incident to King Charles and praised Helen Haines’s work as a local representative, including her commitment to improving the standards of public discourse in Australia. “This violent attack on a much loved and respected sitting member of our federal parliament must be a moment for us to pause and to choose to be better,” she said. “We’ve got to hope that that beautiful heart, that beautiful mind will be strengthened every day by our support and our commitment to be more like Helen as part of this great democracy.” Anthony Albanese and politicians from across federal parliament have expressed shock and anger at the alleged attack on Haines. The incident has sparked calls for changes to politicians’ safety, with security services including the Australian federal police and Asio briefing MPs on the current landscape on Wednesday. View image in fullscreen Independent MP Helen Haines is in a stable condition. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/Reuters Speaking at a vigil in Wodonga on Wednesday evening, Cathy McGowan, who held the seat of Indi before Haines, paid tribute to her friend. “There is another level of grief, different and deeper from the actual violence, from the sorrow, the shame and the hurt,” she said. “It’s about Helen in her role as our elected representative. In attacking her, we intuit that this is an attack on our political system, on our democracy, and especially so for all the supporters who did the democracy work getting Helen elected.” McGowan called for the upcoming Victorian state election campaign to be conducted in a positive and constructive way. Voters go to the polls next month. The community could not let violence win, McGowan implored. “That we ensure the legacy of this attack on Helen will be a stronger, more vibrant and effective democracy, and from a personal perspective, all candidates and especially women, know they can run for office and be safe.” Explore more on these topics Helen Haines Australian politics news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story No bail for alleged Helen Haines attacker as police chief warns of Australia’s ‘febrile’ political environment Soft-spoken David Pocock has big ambitions – but first he wants politicians to ‘double down’ on kindness AFP warns Australia of ‘tsunami of youth crime’ and radicalisation accelerated by AI Australian democracy is usually peaceful. Photograph: Joel Saget/AFP/Getty Images Awards and prizes Canadian publisher Boréal ends relationship with novelist Thélyson Orélien over alleged use of AI Author withdrawn from France’s Prix Goncourt last month has repeatedly denied using artificial intelligence to write novel Agence France-Presse Wed 21 Oct 2026 21.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The publisher of top-selling Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien, who was removed from France’s most prestigious literary prize list last month, has confirmed the author used artificial intelligence to help write his novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was Either That or Die). Orélien has denied allegations that he used AI on his breakthrough novel and, last week, Canadian publisher Les Éditions du Boréal said it was standing by the 38-year-old writer. But on Wednesday, Boréal said it had conducted a further investigation into the allegations. “New information, confirmed over the past few days, indicates that artificial intelligence was used in the writing process” of the novel, a statement from Boréal said. The publisher announced it was “ending its professional relationship” with Orélien. Boréal said it did not know the extent of AI’s use in the writing process “and we will likely never have a definitive answer”. It said it gathered all the working versions of the novel and hired an outside party to analyse various drafts. Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize list Read more “The results obtained this week revealed traces of AI tags in the metadata of certain documents,” Boréal said. Before conducting this analysis, the publisher said it had tried to work with Orélien to gather the evidence necessary to prove his innocence. That effort was inconclusive, and Orélien “subsequently announced that he would not provide any further information,” the publisher said. The novel about migration had been scheduled for translation in more than 20 countries. The book was shrouded in suspicion and withdrawn from the list for France’s book prize the Prix Goncourt , after tests with AI detector Pangram indicated a 100% probability it contained computer-generated text. In a statement to Agence France-Presse earlier this month, Orélien called the allegations “slander and heresy”. “Here and there I did use tools for research, particularly for foreign idioms,” he said in a statement sent exclusively to AFP. “But not a single sentence in this book was created by a machine, nor the meaning or the structure of a story that comes from my gut.” He stood firm on Wednesday, telling the French newspaper Libération he used AI “in the creative process” for “historical research”. “I’ve explained everything to those close to me, but at the moment I don’t think my words count for anything,” he said, adding that what he is now experiencing has “gone way too far”. Orélien said he started writing the book in late 2017 “on the corner of a table” and completed a first draft in 2019 of more than 300 pages, several years before the advent of AI services such as ChatGPT. The author fled his native Haiti after a 2010 earthquake that struck the Caribbean island, already ravaged by poverty and unrest. In response to separate allegations of plagiarism, Orélien admitted to making “unacceptable mistakes” in the past in his writing, without mentioning specifics. “I was just over 20, I was probably a little too impatient, without really understanding how much I still had to learn. I wanted to write, I was reading a lot,” he wrote. “But admiring someone does not give you the right to take, to claim as mine texts that are not my own.” Explore more on these topics Awards and prizes Fiction AI (artificial intelligence) Europe Prix Goncourt Canada France news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: It took the UK destroyer warship HMS Dragon more than three weeks to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone. Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen It took the UK destroyer warship HMS Dragon more than three weeks to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone. Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty Images Defence policy Royal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warn Committee cites shortfalls of submarines and warships and says ‘dramatic progress’ needed by end of decade Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Britain risks failing to deter future Russian aggression in the high north beyond the UK because of shortfalls in the number and availability of Royal Navy submarines and warships, MPs on the defence select committee have said. The committee focused on the slow deployment of HMS Dragon to Cyprus this spring, declining numbers of frigates, and reports that all five Astute-class attack submarines were in dock this summer as evidence of a navy under-resourced for the threat. “The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the high north,” said Tan Dhesi, the committee chair. “Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments.” The high north, the seas beyond Scotland, have become increasingly strategically significant amid growing Russian interest in energy pipelines and undersea cables at a time when Arctic seaways are opening up because of global heating. The navy shadowed a Russian spy ship, the Yantar, operating inside the UK’s economic waters in November and January last year, accusing sailors onboard of trying to map strategic cables and shining lasers at RAF pilots monitoring them. Map of high north Russia also wants to assert control over the emerging northern sea route, a 3,500-mile (5,600km) shipping lane running along the country’s Arctic coast. It is the quickest maritime route from China to Europe, navigable last year for four and half months. The MPs argued the UK needed to make “dramatic progress” before the end of the decade, and they called on the Ministry of Defence to draw up a plan to ensure more warships and submarines are at sea by 2030. The problem would be particularly acute, the committee added, if the US did not support the UK in a crisis, a rare cross-party acknowledgment that under Donald Trump, US military help cannot be relied on, particularly if a small Nato member in the region was threatened or attacked. “There would be critical military gaps if the United States were not involved in countering such [Russian] aggression,” the MPs said, and they argued that the UK, as the next largest Nato military in the region, had to be prepared to increase its navy. It took more than three weeks for HMS Dragon, a destroyer, to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean in March after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone. No warships were available and Dragon had to be hauled out of dry dock to deploy. The navy has five frigates with sonar dedicated to detecting Russian submarines at distance, the committee noted, lower than a target of eight, as ageing warships have been scrapped without replacements coming into service. It could take until 2037 before it reaches its stated requirement, the committee added. None of Britain’s five Astute submarines, also used to track Russian maritime activity, were at sea from June and into the summer. They were in dock for a mixture of short-term and long-term refits, the committee noted, and they also lack the capability to operate under ice, unlike their Russian equivalents, although certification exercises are in progress. However, no significant extra money is expected to be available for defence until the next decade, with Andy Burnham’s government committed to medium-term spending plans agreed under Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer. Though Starmer agreed to lift defence spending by about £30bn a year to 3.5% of GDP in 2035, he would only sign off spending to the lower level of 2.7% by 2030. That prompted the resignation of John Healey as defence secretary, only for him to return as chancellor under Burnham, with the old spending plans intact. In response to the report, an MoD spokesperson highlighted a recent £330m investment to protect undersea infrastructure, and noted that Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, had visited Iceland this month and watched how HMS St Albans, a frigate, tracked Russian submarines in the north Atlantic. “We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses,” they added.
